style_1_icd10.name: Siderosis of eye, right eye
style_1_icd10.chapter: VII. Diseases of the eye and ear (H00-H95)

clinical_targets.goal: Target IOP reduction of 20–30% from baseline (< 18 mmHg)
Stabilization or improvement of Snellen visual acuity (BCVA)
Zero progressive visual field loss on automated perimetry

steps_summary: Step 1: Step 1: First-Line Therapy: Conservative Foundation & Targeted Monotherapy
Step 2: Step 2: Second-Line / Dual Add-On Therapy (Inadequate Response to Step 1)
Step 3: Step 3: Third-Line / Advanced Specialty Therapy & Multidisciplinary Escalation
Step 4: Step 4: Refractory / Salvage Protocols & Interventional / Inpatient Care

steps.title: Step 1: First-Line Therapy: Conservative Foundation & Targeted Monotherapy
steps.rationale: Initial management of Eye Diseases focuses on non-pharmacological foundations, patient education, elimination of precipitating triggers, and initiating evidence-based first-line monotherapy. Treatment should begin at the lowest effective dose with periodic reassessment.

drug_classes.dosing: Standard clinical care protocol under medical supervision.
drug_classes.pearls: Establish baseline clinical parameters and educate patient on trigger avoidance and early warning signs.

steps.title: Step 2: Second-Line / Dual Add-On Therapy (Inadequate Response to Step 1)
steps.rationale: For patients with persistent symptoms, partial response, or disease progression after 4–8 weeks of Step 1 therapy, escalate by titrating to the maximum tolerated dose or adding a complementary second-line agent with a distinct mechanism of action.

drug_classes.role: Dose optimization and complementary therapeutic escalation.
drug_classes.dosing: Titrate to target clinical biomarker thresholds under specialist guidance.
drug_classes.pearls: Evaluate patient compliance and consider secondary causes of treatment resistance.

steps.title: Step 3: Third-Line / Advanced Specialty Therapy & Multidisciplinary Escalation
steps.rationale: Patients with severe, recalcitrant, or treatment-refractory Eye Diseases require multidisciplinary subspecialist evaluation and consideration of advanced therapies (biologics, targeted small molecules, immunosuppressive regimens, or specialized combination protocols).

drug_classes.role: Multidisciplinary tertiary intervention for refractory disease.
drug_classes.pearls: Consult subspecialty guidelines and consider therapeutic drug monitoring where applicable.

steps.title: Step 4: Refractory / Salvage Protocols & Interventional / Inpatient Care
steps.rationale: Reserved for treatment-resistant, acute progressive, or complicated disease. Protocol includes parenteral salvage therapies, procedural or surgical interventions, inpatient stabilization, and long-term rehabilitation.

drug_classes.role: Rescue intervention for complicated or refractory Eye Diseases.
drug_classes.dosing: Hospital or tertiary center procedural protocol.
drug_classes.pearls: Careful risk-benefit assessment by a multidisciplinary clinical care team.

pearls: Establish baseline clinical parameters and educate patient on trigger avoidance and early warning signs.

special_populations.renal_impairment: Topical ocular drops have minimal systemic absorption; nasolacrimal occlusion further reduces absorption.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Oral carbonic anhydrase inhibitors require caution in severe hepatic impairment.
special_populations.pregnancy_lactation: Brimonidine and topical beta-blockers used with nasolacrimal occlusion if strictly necessary.
special_populations.elderly: Evaluate manual dexterity for drop instillation; monitor systemic effects of ocular beta-blockers (bradycardia).

style_3_monograph.summary: What diseases can affect the eye? Even if your eyes feel healthy, you could have a problem and not know it. That's why regular eye exams are so important. Refractive errors are the most common type of vision problem that makes it hard to see clearly. But some eye conditions or diseases don't have any symptoms and can lead to a permanent loss of vision . Some common eye diseases and conditions include: Cataracts , which happens when the clear lens in the front of your eye becomes cloudy. Cataracts are common as you get older and can lead to vision loss. Optic nerve disorders , which includes glaucoma . Glaucoma usually happens when the fluid pressure inside your eyes slowly rises. Retinal disorders , which are problems with the nerve layer at the back of your eye. Macular degeneration , which is a disease that destroys your sharp, central vision. Diabetic eye problems , which can cause vision loss and blindness. Conjunctivitis , which is an infection also known as pink eye . It can cause pink or red itchy eyes. Some types of pink eye can spread very easily. What are the symptoms of eye diseases? Some eye conditions and diseases do not always have symptoms. Early detection through a comprehensive dilated eye exam could help your eye care provider detect diseases in the early stages. Proper treatment could help slow or prevent vision loss. Get regular eye exams and call your eye care professional right away if you notice any of these symptoms: A sudden change in vision Everything looks dim Flashes of light Eye pain Double vision Fluid coming from your eye Inflammation (swelling) Who is more likely to develop eye diseases? Getting older increases your risk of some eye diseases. Other things that may put you at a higher risk of some eye diseases can include if you: Are overweight or obese Have a family history of eye disease Are African American, Hispanic, or Native American Have certain health conditions such as Diabetic eye problems , or high blood pressure What are the treatments for eye diseases? Treatment may depend on the eye condition or disease but can include: A new prescription for eyeglasses or contacts Use of bright lights or magnifying lenses for reading and other activities Medicines Prescription eye drops or ointments Laser treatment Surgery Depending on your eye condition or disease, treatment may slow vision loss but may not restore vision. Talk to your provider about what treatment is best for you. Can eye diseases be prevented? Your best defense is to have regular checkups. Be sure to tell your provider if any eye diseases run in your family. You can also help take care of your vision by making lifestyle changes to lower your risk of health conditions that can cause vision problems. This could include by: Protecting your eyes from the sun Wearing protective eyewear while using tools or playing certain sports Getting regular physical activity Staying at a healthy weight Quitting smoking (or not starting) Eating a healthy diet NIH: National Eye Institute
